title: Skull (frontal bone)
fact: The skull has 22 bones; all but the mandible are locked together by sutures.

title: Parietal bone
fact: The two parietal bones form the roof and sides of the skull.

title: Occipital bone
fact: The spinal cord leaves the skull through the foramen magnum in this bone.

title: Temporal bone
fact: Holds the smallest bones in the body, the ear ossicles, deep inside.

title: Mandible
fact: The jaw is the only skull bone that moves, and the strongest bone of the face.

title: Maxilla
fact: The two maxillae hold the upper teeth and form the floor of each eye socket.

title: Zygomatic bone
fact: The cheekbone; it forms the outer wall of the eye socket.

title: Nasal bone
fact: Only the bridge of the nose is bone; the rest of its shape is cartilage.

title: Teeth
fact: Enamel, the outer layer of teeth, is the hardest substance in the human body.

title: Ear ossicles
fact: The stapes, about 3 mm long, is the smallest bone in the body.

title: Hyoid bone
fact: The only bone that doesn't touch another bone; it anchors the tongue.

title: Clavicle
fact: The collarbone is the most commonly broken bone in the body.

title: Scapula
fact: The shoulder blade attaches to the trunk only through muscles and the clavicle.

title: Sternum
fact: The breastbone has three parts: manubrium, body and xiphoid process.

title: Ribs
fact: 12 pairs: 7 attach straight to the sternum, 3 indirectly, 2 'float' free.

title: Cervical vertebrae
fact: Seven neck vertebrae, the same count as in a giraffe.

title: Thoracic vertebrae
fact: Twelve vertebrae, each paired with a rib.

title: Lumbar vertebrae
fact: The five largest vertebrae carry most of the upper body's weight.

title: Sacrum
fact: Five vertebrae that fuse into one bone between ages 18 and 30.

title: Coccyx
fact: The tailbone: 3–5 small fused vertebrae.

title: Pelvis (hip bone)
fact: Each hip bone is three bones fused together: ilium, ischium and pubis.

title: Humerus
fact: The 'funny bone' tingle is the ulnar nerve crossing the back of the humerus's lower end.

title: Radius
fact: Rotates around the ulna to turn the palm up or down.

title: Ulna
fact: Its hook-shaped top, the olecranon, is the point of your elbow.

title: Hand bones
fact: Each hand has 27 bones: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges.

title: Femur
fact: The thighbone is the longest and strongest bone in the body.

title: Patella
fact: The kneecap is the largest sesamoid bone, a bone that forms inside a tendon.

title: Tibia
fact: The shinbone carries about 85% of the body's weight through the lower leg.

title: Fibula
fact: Carries little weight; surgeons sometimes harvest it as a bone graft.

title: Foot bones
fact: Each foot has 26 bones; the calcaneus (heel bone) is the largest.

title: Laryngeal cartilage
fact: The thyroid cartilage forms the Adam's apple.

title: Frontalis
fact: Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead.

title: Temporalis
fact: A fan-shaped chewing muscle you can feel at your temple when you clench.

title: Masseter
fact: Relative to its size, one of the strongest muscles in the body; it closes the jaw.

title: Orbicularis oculi
fact: Closes the eyelids; it fires every time you blink.

title: Orbicularis oris
fact: The ring muscle that purses the lips.

title: Zygomaticus
fact: The main smiling muscle; it pulls the mouth corners up and out.

title: Sternocleidomastoid
fact: Turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it.

title: Trapezius
fact: Moves, rotates and steadies the shoulder blades.

title: Deltoid
fact: Lifts the arm. Its three heads move it forward, sideways and back.

title: Pectoralis major
fact: Pulls the arm across the chest; the main muscle used in push-ups.
anchor: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle.r

title: Pectoralis minor
fact: Lies under pectoralis major and steadies the scapula.

title: Serratus anterior
fact: The 'boxer's muscle': it drives the shoulder blade forward when you punch.

title: Latissimus dorsi
fact: The widest muscle of the back; it powers pull-ups and swimming strokes.

title: Rhomboids
fact: Squeeze the shoulder blades together.

title: Rotator cuff
fact: Four muscles that hold the ball of the humerus in its shallow socket.

title: Biceps brachii
fact: Bends the elbow and turns the palm up, the motion of turning a screwdriver.

title: Triceps brachii
fact: Straightens the elbow; it makes up about two thirds of the upper arm's bulk.

title: Brachioradialis
fact: Bends the elbow most strongly when the thumb points up, as in a hammer curl.

title: Forearm flexors
fact: Most of the muscles that bend your fingers sit in the forearm and act through long tendons.

title: Forearm extensors
fact: Straighten the wrist and fingers; overuse causes 'tennis elbow'.

title: Hand muscles
match: (lumbrical|interossei|opponens|abductor pollicis brevis|adductor pollicis|flexor digiti minimi of hand|abductor digiti minimi of hand|flexor pollicis brevis)
fact: Small muscles inside the hand provide fine control. The thumb has its own set.

title: Rectus abdominis
fact: The 'six-pack'; tendon bands across it create the segments.

title: External oblique
fact: Twists and bends the trunk; its fibres run like hands in front pockets.

title: Internal oblique / transversus
fact: Deep layers that brace the abdomen like a natural corset.

title: Intercostals
fact: Muscles between the ribs that help you breathe.

title: Diaphragm
fact: The main breathing muscle; it flattens to draw air into the lungs.

title: Erector spinae
fact: Long columns along the spine that keep you upright.

title: Gluteus maximus
fact: The largest muscle in the body; it extends the hip when you climb or stand.

title: Gluteus medius / minimus
fact: Keep the pelvis level each time you stand on one leg while walking.

title: Iliopsoas
fact: The strongest hip flexor; it lifts the thigh toward the trunk.

title: Sartorius
fact: The longest muscle in the body; it crosses the thigh diagonally.

title: Quadriceps
fact: Four muscles that straighten the knee; together the strongest group in the body.

title: Adductors
fact: Pull the legs together; 'groin strains' tear these.

title: Hamstrings
fact: Three muscles that bend the knee and extend the hip.

title: Tensor fasciae latae
fact: Tightens the iliotibial band to steady the knee.

title: Tibialis anterior
fact: Lifts the foot. If it is weak, the toes drag ('foot drop').

title: Gastrocnemius
fact: The calf muscle; it joins the soleus in the Achilles tendon.

title: Soleus
fact: Called the 'second heart' because it pumps blood back up the leg.

title: Achilles tendon
fact: The thickest and strongest tendon in the body.

title: Fibularis muscles
fact: Turn the sole outward and steady the ankle.

title: Platysma
fact: A thin sheet over the front of the neck that tenses its skin.

title: Tongue muscles
fact: The tongue is a group of eight muscles with no bone inside.

title: Eye muscles
fact: Six muscles aim each eye and make some of the fastest movements in the body.

title: Aorta
fact: The largest artery: about 2.5 cm wide where it leaves the heart.

title: Coronary arteries
fact: Supply the heart muscle itself; a blockage here causes a heart attack.

title: Common carotid artery
fact: The pulse you feel at the side of your neck.

title: Internal carotid artery
fact: Supplies most of the blood to the front of the brain and the eye.

title: External carotid artery
fact: Supplies the face, scalp and jaws.

title: Vertebral artery
fact: Runs up through holes in the neck vertebrae to the back of the brain.

title: Circle of Willis
fact: A ring of arteries under the brain that reroutes blood if one artery is blocked.

title: Subclavian artery
fact: Carries blood under the collarbone into each arm.

title: Axillary artery
fact: The armpit section of the main arm artery.

title: Brachial artery
fact: The artery a blood-pressure cuff presses on.

title: Radial artery
fact: The pulse you take at the wrist, on the thumb side.

title: Ulnar artery
fact: Joins the radial artery in arches across the palm.

title: Pulmonary trunk & arteries
match: pulmonary (trunk|artery)|artery of (right|left) lung|lobar artery|segmental artery of
fact: The only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood, from the heart to the lungs.

title: Coeliac trunk
fact: Feeds the stomach, liver and spleen.

title: Renal artery
fact: About a fifth of the heart's output goes to the kidneys.

title: Mesenteric arteries
fact: Supply the intestines.

title: Common iliac artery
fact: The aorta splits into these two at about navel level.

title: Femoral artery
fact: The main artery of the thigh; you can feel its pulse in the groin.

title: Popliteal artery
fact: Runs behind the knee.

title: Tibial arteries
fact: Supply the lower leg; the posterior one has a pulse behind the ankle bone.

title: Dorsalis pedis
fact: A pulse on top of the foot that doctors check for circulation.

title: Superior vena cava
fact: Returns blood from the head, neck and arms to the heart.

title: Inferior vena cava
fact: The largest vein; it returns blood from the lower body.

title: Internal jugular vein
fact: Drains the brain; sometimes visible pulsing in the neck.

title: External jugular vein
fact: Often visible bulging in the neck when you strain.

title: Dural venous sinuses
fact: Channels between layers of the brain's outer membrane that drain blood from the brain.

title: Subclavian vein
fact: A common entry point for central IV lines.

title: Brachiocephalic vein
fact: The left and right ones join to form the superior vena cava.

title: Cephalic vein
fact: A superficial vein on the thumb side of the arm.

title: Basilic vein
fact: A superficial vein on the little-finger side of the arm.

title: Median cubital vein
fact: The vein at the inner elbow used for most blood draws.

title: Pulmonary veins
match: pulmonary vein|vein of (right|left) lung|lobar vein|segmental vein
fact: The only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood, from the lungs to the heart.

title: Hepatic portal vein
fact: Carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut to the liver for processing.

title: Renal vein
fact: Returns filtered blood from the kidneys.

title: Common iliac vein
fact: The two join to form the inferior vena cava.

title: Femoral vein
fact: The main deep vein of the thigh.

title: Great saphenous vein
fact: The longest vein in the body, ankle to groin; often used for heart bypass grafts.

title: Small saphenous vein
fact: Runs up the back of the calf.

title: Azygos vein
fact: Drains the chest wall and can bypass a blocked vena cava.

title: Heart
fact: Beats about 100,000 times a day and pumps roughly 7,000 litres of blood.

title: Lungs
fact: The right lung has three lobes and the left has two, leaving room for the heart.

title: Left lung
fact: Has a notch, the cardiac notch, where the heart sits.

title: Trachea
fact: The windpipe, kept open by 16–20 C-shaped rings of cartilage.

title: Bronchi
fact: The airways branch about 23 times before reaching the air sacs.

title: Liver
fact: The largest internal organ. It handles more than 500 tasks and can regrow lost tissue.

title: Gallbladder
fact: Stores bile, which helps digest fat.

title: Stomach
fact: Its acid is about as strong as lemon juice or stronger; a mucus layer keeps it from digesting itself.

title: Oesophagus
fact: Muscle waves push food to the stomach in about 7 seconds, even upside down.

title: Spleen
fact: Filters old red blood cells and stores immune cells.

title: Pancreas
fact: Makes digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.

title: Kidneys
fact: Together they filter about 180 litres of blood plasma a day into 1–2 litres of urine.

title: Adrenal glands
fact: Sit on top of the kidneys and make adrenaline and cortisol.

title: Ureters
fact: Muscular tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

title: Urinary bladder
fact: Usually holds about 400–600 ml.

title: Urethra
fact: Carries urine out of the body; it is about 4 cm long in women and 20 cm in men.

title: Duodenum
fact: The first 25 cm of the small intestine, where bile and pancreatic juice enter.

title: Small intestine
fact: About 6 m long. Its folds give it a surface area of roughly 30 m².

title: Large intestine
fact: Absorbs water and is home to trillions of gut bacteria.

title: Appendix
fact: May act as a reserve of good gut bacteria.

title: Thyroid gland
fact: A butterfly-shaped gland whose hormones set the body's metabolic rate.

title: Parathyroid glands
fact: Four rice-grain-sized glands that control blood calcium.

title: Thymus
fact: Trains T cells. It is largest in childhood and mostly fat by old age.

title: Salivary glands
fact: Together they make about 1–1.5 litres of saliva a day.

title: Tongue
fact: Its surface carries about 2,000–8,000 taste buds.

title: Pharynx & larynx
fact: The epiglottis flaps over the airway each time you swallow.

title: Eye
fact: The retina holds about 120 million rods and 6 million cones.

title: Pituitary gland
fact: A pea-sized 'master gland' that controls most other hormone glands.

title: Pineal gland
fact: Makes melatonin, which helps regulate sleep.

title: Testis
fact: Makes sperm (about 1,500 a second) and testosterone.

title: Prostate
fact: A walnut-sized gland that adds fluid to semen.

title: Penis
fact: Erection happens when its spongy tissue fills with blood.

title: Uterus
fact: A muscular organ about the size of a pear; in pregnancy it grows about 500-fold.

title: Ovary
fact: Each one is born holding about a million egg cells.

title: Uterine (fallopian) tube
fact: Fertilisation usually happens here; finger-like fimbriae catch the released egg.

title: Vagina
fact: A muscular, elastic canal from the cervix to the outside of the body.

title: Mammary gland
fact: Has 15–20 lobes, each draining through its own duct to the nipple.

title: Frontal lobe
fact: Handles planning, decisions and personality. The precentral gyrus drives voluntary movement.

title: Parietal lobe
fact: Processes touch and body position; the postcentral gyrus is a map of the skin.

title: Temporal lobe
fact: Processes hearing, language comprehension and memory.

title: Occipital lobe
fact: The visual cortex; damage here can cause blindness even when the eyes are healthy.

title: Limbic system
fact: Handles emotion and memory. The hippocampus forms new memories.

title: Insula
fact: Senses the body's inner state: heartbeat, hunger, disgust.

title: Corpus callosum
fact: About 200 million nerve fibres connecting the left and right hemispheres.

title: Basal ganglia
fact: Help start and smooth movement; they are damaged in Parkinson's disease.

title: Thalamus & hypothalamus
fact: The thalamus relays sensory signals to the cortex; the hypothalamus controls hunger, temperature and hormones.

title: Cerebellum
fact: Holds more than half the brain's neurons in a tenth of its volume, and coordinates movement.

title: Brainstem
fact: Controls breathing, heart rate and consciousness.

title: Ventricles
fact: Hollow spaces that make about 500 ml of cerebrospinal fluid a day.

title: Spinal cord
fact: About 45 cm long and roughly as thick as a finger.
